2 Dads, 3 Babies

By: Ben Dwork | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Families come in all shapes and sizes, but what happens when the traditional notion of a nuclear family begins to shift as same sex parenting and surrogacy becomes more prevalent?

Unique Selling Point:
Christo and Theo Menelaou made international news when their surrogate delivered triplets in July 2016. Now Carte Blanche brings an exclusive update on the triplet’s progress, their first birthday, and delves into issues surrounding surrogacy and same sex parenting.

Summary:
In “2 Dads, 3 Babies,” we’ll spend a day in the life of Christo Menelaou, who owns a construction business in Pretoria. A wedding ring on his finger indicates he’s happily married, and as we arrive home with him, we meet his partner -- Theo. No ordinary same sex couple, last year Christo and Theo fulfilled their quest to become parents with the help of surrogate. She just happened to deliver triplets: Joshua, and twins Zoe and Kate. As we spend a day with Menelaou family, we’ll see the human stories behind same sex parenting and surrogacy. Though same sex parents still face stigma in society, the tide is beginning to change.

We’ll take a step back and explain the legal process that South Africa has in place for surrogacy and then speak with a researcher who's done extensive work looking at the changing notion of ‘family’ in South Africa and what that means to society. Recent studies have shown no significant difference between children raised in same sex homes and those raised in heterosexual ones. The findings are that as long as the core relationship between the parents is strong and healthy, children will thrive. The notion of family as a man, woman, and children is currently in a state of upheaval. And with that, we’ll meet two adults who are the product of same sex homes: brothers with 2 lesbian mothers who were born via invitro fertilization in the 80s -- Samuel, who is straight and now married to a woman, and his brother Ben, who is gay. Samuel now works for a gay rights advocacy group, doing work that he says comes naturally to him since he spent his formative years educating others and helping them shed their homophobia.

Finally, we’ll return to the Menelaou family. Christo, Theo, Joshua, Kate, and Zoe are just starting out in this world. With research and case studies on their side for a bright future, will the rest of South Africa be there as well?


Further information:
We open on the Menelaou family -- Christo, Theo, and their triplets: Joshua, and twins Kate and Zoe. As we hear from the couple about the journey to becoming fathers, we’ll also get to experience a day in the life with the family. The truly unique way they all came together -- through the generosity of a woman, who would become their surrogate, that they met at the trial for their former neighbor and friend Oscar Pistorius -- may be starkly different from the “traditional family” model, but theirs is just the same. Infants fuss and make a mess, and stressed out parents figure it out on the fly. We’ll watch them prepare for a big day: the triplets first birthday, what they’ve decided will be a lowkey affair with just photos and cake.

We’ll then hear from Adele Van Der Walt, a lawyer specializing in medical law and surrogacy. She’ll walk us through the legal aspects of the arrangement, especially as they pertain to same sex couples: everything from how a surrogate is connected to a couple to ethics issues that may arise, and even emotional issues. Though the legal process for surrogacy in South Africa is quite regimented, the psychological and emotional side of it is anything but.

Back with the Menelaou family, Christo and Theo talk about daughter Kate, who was born with a heart condition that required open heart surgery in November 2016 (when she was only a few months old; they had to wait until she was 4kg to proceed with the surgery) and will require a follow up procedure next month. Though the joy of becoming fathers has provided for an intensely emotional year, Kate’s health has also been a major concern, demonstrating that a parent’s concern for their child’s health is universal, no matter what your sexual orientation.

Carien Lubbe-De Beer, a professor of psychology at the University of Pretoria -- now based in New Zealand with her family -- has been researching the changing notion of ‘family’ in South Africa for many years, especially as it relates to same sex couples and their children. She’s published numerous papers detailing her work, including how “gay people are increasingly opting for motherhood and fatherhood by creating families of their own or by continuing to live with their children from former heterosexual relationships.” In the case studies that follow, we’ll meet now-grown children of both types of same sex families and hear their experiences growing up.

Case studies will demonstrate that there’s no one single type of this new family. Samuel Shapiro was born to lesbian mothers through in vitro fertilization. Now, at the age of 29 and married to a woman, he’s dedicated his career to being an activist to advance equality and freedom in southern Africa with a particular emphasis on sexual orientation and gender identity. Not only will he speak of his personal experiences growing up in a same sex household, he’ll be a key voice in explaining how we can all do our part to help shed the stigma that is still too-often attached to families with same sex parents. We’ll also speak to his older brother Ben, who is gay, and what it was like growing up in a household with two moms and no significant male figures in his life. How did his upbringing shape who he’s become today?

With the Meneloaus one final time, we see Christo and Theo working together to take care of the triplets. We’ll hear about their hopes and dreams for the children, tempered yet with some nerves about Kate’s upcoming surgery. Theirs may look different and may have come into being in a different way, but their family is just like any other. [Possibly end with Samuel Shapiro: “Gay parents are starting to be accepted… Not only can the world be different, but it’s happening. Change is inevitable.”]

Press Release:


Families come in all shapes and sizes. But what happens when surrogacy and same sex parenting changes the traditional notion of family. @Devi Sankaree Govender meets two dads who have turned the traditional idea of family on its head.

Script:


Music. (00:00 - 00:11)
DG: Becoming a parent is one of life’s greatest gifts. But for many, just the act of even starting a family is a journey fraught with difficulties.
DG VO: Christo Menelaou owns a construction business in Pretoria, and had always wanted a large family.
DG: Had you always wanted to be a dad, or was that something you discovered later in life?
CM: I think I was in pre-school, not 7 or 8 years old, and I’d always look after the neighbor’s babies and stuff. And I said I want hundreds of children. I loved it.
DG VO: Theo Menelaou is Christo’s husband. They’ve been together for 10 years.
TM: I always knew that I wanted kids and a family. It’s difficult being labeled as someone, you never think you’re different from anyone else, especially if you’ve got a reference from a family you grew up with. I mean, we went through the adoption process, because I said it doesn’t matter if it’s your own child or another child. And I think through the whole process, it, it, we became aware of it more and more that, um, it’s difficult for same sex couples to adopt.
DG: The South African constitution is one of the most progressive in the world. Same sex couples have been allowed to legally marry for over ten years. // But if they wanted to start a family, it’s a complicated and lengthy process.
CM: We did all of our applications and stuff, and you won’t hear anything back. And I phoned the lady one day, and I said ‘What is going on?’ She said, ‘Listen here, off the record, a straight couple will always have preference above you guys. So, go on. I’m not saying give up hope, but it’s gonna be years.’
TM: We actually gave up, with, that day we gave up on the whole process. And we said, you know what - we’ll keep on loving each other for the rest of our lives, and um, we’ll have family with my brother and sister, and, um, we’ll just keep to that.
CM: I were involved in a court case, and after we, the last day of the court case, all the witnesses came together and like had a get together. One lady asked me, ‘Why are you so grumpy? Aren’t you glad we’re done with it?’ And I said, ‘No, you know, I spoke to that social worker, and she said, um, you’re actually wasting your time.’ And the lady just looked at me, and said, ‘Why do you want to adopt a child? Why do you want to raise somebody else’s child?’ And I’m like: ‘No, because we want children.’ ‘But have your own.’ And I’m like, huh? ‘Do a surrogate.’
DG VO: A short time after that encounter, Christo and Theo received a message that would change their lives. A woman reached out, offering to be their surrogate.
TM: Since we got the message, there was actually a period of two weeks that’s gone by. Which, I was just too afraid to answer the lady. And I said to Christo, ‘I don’t know what we should do.’
DG VO: Despite their fears, the volunteer had no problem being a surrogate for a gay couple.
TM: She had three very easy pregnancies. And, um, she believes if she can help someone with the blessing of life, um, then she will actually do it.
DG VO: Though surrogacy is becoming a more common option, some couples resort to other methods. Brothers Sam and Ben Shapiro share their story.
DG: Did you see yourself when you grew, growing up, did you see yourself as -- I have two moms.
SS: I always knew that my family was different. How I experienced that wasn’t necessarily that, that as any different to any other family.
DG: You and your brother were born via… // SS: Artificial insemination. // DG: Right. And that was a big deal then. Now it’s… what happens.
SS: It was illegal then. Both my parents I think always wanted children. Um, so it never, it never entered their head they wouldn’t have children at some point in their life.
DG VO: Sam and his wife live a short distance from his brother Ben and Ben’s boyfriend. Both Ben and Sam were conceived using sperm from an anonymous donor.
BS: The way they went about it was what they called the double blind system. A system that they, I think my mom did research and found that it was being practiced in America. Where you actually, the, the, the two people interested in having the kid go to someone who goes to someone who goes to a fourth person who then provides the, the semen, and it gets passed back down the line to the first one. The objective of that being that should either of those two people want to find out who the other one is, they have to go through two people to actually, uh, get there. Which provides the anonymity that both parties actually wanted.
DG: Did you have any idea of how to conduct a heterosexual relationship?
SS: [Laughs] None at all. Um, no, I struggled. I won’t lie. I thought, I mean I had girlfriends along the way, but I was good with women, but very friendly with women, and men I was terrible with. I didn’t understand gender norms as well as I could see my friends around me understood it.
DG: There’s very little research in South Africa about same sex household, but international research shows that same sex households are just as suited to raising children as heterosexual ones.
DG VO: Professor Carien Lubbe-De Beer, formerly of the University of Pretoria, is one of the few researchers compiling data on same sex parenting in South Africa.
DG: Is there a stigma to being attached to a single sex family, for the children and for the parents?
CL: I think as with any minority group, um, you’re different than the norm, you’re different than the mainstream, and people are, maybe due to not knowing, they are afraid of what’s this and then they go back to more fundamental core values
DG: Perhaps the point is that the traditional definition of family is just… Traditional. It’s not new, and it’s not 2017. And that’s got to change.
CL: And I think families are ever-changing. And we need to, we need to adapt to that. And we need to embrace the creativity of the different ways in which we can raise children. 40%, um, live with just their mothers, and 23%, um, only live with people that’s not even biologically related to them.
DG VO: Even with a volunteer surrogate, Christo and Theo still had to approach the court to make an application for surrogacy.
DG VO: Adele Van Der Walt is a practicing attorney specializing in medical law and one of the few experts on surrogacy law.
DG: Are you seeing more and more same sex couples for surrogacy?
AW: Definitely. Definitely. Since we’ve got the act, there’s legal clarity, certainty, for all parties. You approach court before the in vitro fertilization takes place, or the embryo transfer. They get a court order, and that court order confirms any baby or babies born from that relationship and contract is the lawful child of the intended parents, being the gay couple.
DG: After 3 in vitro procedures and no viable pregnancy, the Menelaous went back to court.
DG VO: On their fifth attempt, their surrogate fell pregnant… three times over.
DG: What was that moment like when you found out you were going to have triplets?
DM: [Laughing] I just laughed. I haven’t stopped giggling. And my husband said a few very long swear words.
TM: We went to the lady. She started scanning, and it was, this is number one, this is number two, and she was juggling around, and then it was number three.
DG VO: The happy news was short lived, as they would find out a few weeks later during a routine test/ appointment.
TM: On 10 weeks, the doctor said to us, ‘Listen guys, this is not a happy day for me, but you guys need to abort.’
CM: Multiple pregnancies, especially triplets, is very high risk. They thought the one baby was piggybacking on the other baby, and one will be late in the pregnancy, let’s say 28, 25 weeks cause a total miscarriage.
TM: He said, ‘You know the safest is to let go of the twins and to keep on with, with the single pregnancy.’
TM: And, um, he actually booked a termination date for us, for the twins, which was a week later.
TM: And when we walked out of there, we were shattered. And we said, you know, but we just can’t do this.
DG VO: The couple sought other opinions. A subsequent scan showed that the risk of miscarriage was minimal. Their surrogate would help them make the final decision.
CM: We as parents, as the, the parents only from when the babies is born. The surrogate has got all rights which they still in the stomach. So if she decided on 12 weeks to terminate, she was legally allowed. Um, it’s not our, it’s not our choice. She always stood back and said, ‘I’m just the oven. It’s your decision.’ So, we’re blessed with our surrogate.
DG VO: In July 2016, Christo and Theo’s surrogate gave birth to a boy -- Joshua -- and twin girls -- Zoe and Kate.
DG VO: What makes their situation unique is that both fathers are genetically related to one or two of the children -- Christo to Joshua, and Theo to Zoe and Kate.
DG VO: However, Zoe, one of the twin girls, was born with a heart condition that would prove more urgent than either of the fathers realized.
TM: It was end of August, um, she crashed. At home. The one morning. And I rushed off to hospital close by. I didn’t even put her in the car seat. Um, I held her against my chest just to make sure she breathes. And she’s there, that I could actually feel her. And, um, yeah after working on her for 3 hours, they airlifted her to the hospital in Johannesburg.
DG VO: After this initial scare, Zoe would undergo open heart surgery to begin repairing the defects in her heart.
CM: The surgery was a 2 hour surgery, which ended up and 8 and a half hour surgery. And they couldn’t even close her chest open, they left the chest open and just closed it with plaster. They told us we have to prepare ourselves for the worst.
DG VO: Zoe would pull through, but she would require future surgeries to fully address her medical issues.
TM: But I think when you’re there, it’s like the world is ending and you just don’t know where to go. Um, because you’re helpless. I mean, there’s nothing you can do to make this better.
CM: She’s gonna have another follow up surgery. We not prepared, but we know about it. In 2 weeks time.
DG VO: While society seems to be adapting well to the Menelaous and the Shapiros, others in South Africa still face obstacles.
CL: It has been quite tricky to make inroads into the lower socioeconomic strata, and, um, especially the, in terms of race. But just people also fearing for their lives. It’s really difficult in some areas of South Africa that people are afraid to be who they are, um, with the violence and the possibility of losing your life.
DG VO: Back at the Menelaou home, Christo and Theo’s family is like any other.
CM: Our surrogate is still, there’s an open door for her. She stays very nearby.
DG VO: But their surrogate has her own family and children, and though she gave birth to them, she isn’t the triplets’ mother.
DG: What advice do you have for other same sex couples that want to start a family?
CM: My advice would be go for it. There’s nothing different. Um, we’ve got the same rights, we’ve got the same heart. The other day, me and Theo said, we said like, we’re gonna become like grandparents one day. We didn’t thought about that. Like a few weeks ago, like oh no, they gonna be opa and oma. [Laughing]
TM: I will tell them to never look back. Because that will be the best decision they will ever make. There is nothing better that can happen to your life than being blessed with a child.

DG VO: Christo Menelaou owns a construction business in Pretoria, and had always wanted a large family. DG: Had you always wanted to be a dad, or was that something you discovered later in life? DG VO: Theo Menelaou is Christo’s husband. They’ve been together for 10 years. TM: I always knew that I wanted kids and a family. It’s difficult being labeled as someone, you never think you’re different from anyone else, especially if you’ve got a reference from a family you grew up with. I mean, we went through the adoption process, because I said it doesn’t matter if it’s your own child or another child. And I think through the whole process, it, it, we became aware of it more and more that, um, it’s difficult for same sex couples to adopt. DG: The South African constitution is one of the most progressive in the world. Same sex couples have been allowed to legally marry for over ten years. // But if they wanted to start a family, it’s a complicated and lengthy process. CM: We did all of our applications and stuff, and you won’t hear anything back. And I phoned the lady one day, and I said ‘What is going on?’ She said, ‘Listen here, off the record, a straight couple will always have preference above you guys. So, go on. I’m not saying give up hope, but it’s gonna be years.’ TM: We actually gave up, with, that day we gave up on the whole process. And we said, you know what - we’ll keep on loving each other for the rest of our lives, and um, we’ll have family with my brother and sister, and, um, we’ll just keep to that. CM: I were involved in a court case, and after we, the last day of the court case, all the witnesses came together and like had a get together. One lady asked me, ‘Why are you so grumpy? Aren’t you glad we’re done with it?’ And I said, ‘No, you know, I spoke to that social worker, and she said, um, you’re actually wasting your time.’ And the lady just looked at me, and said, ‘Why do you want to adopt a child? Why do you want to raise somebody else’s child?’ And I’m like: ‘No, because we want children.’ ‘But have your own.’ And I’m like, huh? ‘Do a surrogate.’ DG VO: A short time after that encounter, Christo and Theo received a message that would change their lives. A woman reached out, offering to be their surrogate. TM: Since we got the message, there was actually a period of two weeks that’s gone by. Which, I was just too afraid to answer the lady. And I said to Christo, ‘I don’t know what we should do.’ DG VO: Despite their fears, the volunteer had no problem being a surrogate for a gay couple. TM: She had three very easy pregnancies. And, um, she believes if she can help someone with the blessing of life, um, then she will actually do it. DG VO: Though surrogacy is becoming a more common option, some couples resort to other methods. Brothers Sam and Ben Shapiro share their story. DG: Did you see yourself when you grew, growing up, did you see yourself as -- I have two moms. SS: I always knew that my family was different. How I experienced that wasn’t necessarily that, that as any different to any other family. DG: You and your brother were born via… // SS: Artificial insemination. // DG: Right. And that was a big deal then. Now it’s… what happens. SS: It was illegal then. Both my parents I think always wanted children. Um, so it never, it never entered their head they wouldn’t have children at some point in their life. DG VO: Sam and his wife live a short distance from his brother Ben and Ben’s boyfriend. Both Ben and Sam were conceived using sperm from an anonymous donor. BS: The way they went about it was what they called the double blind system. A system that they, I think my mom did research and found that it was being practiced in America. Where you actually, the, the, the two people interested in having the kid go to someone who goes to someone who goes to a fourth person who then provides the, the semen, and it gets passed back down the line to the first one. The objective of that being that should either of those two people want to find out who the other one is, they have to go through two people to actually, uh, get there. Which provides the anonymity that both parties actually wanted. DG: Did you have any idea of how to conduct a heterosexual relationship? SS: [Laughs] None at all. Um, no, I struggled. I won’t lie. I thought, I mean I had girlfriends along the way, but I was good with women, but very friendly with women, and men I was terrible with. I didn’t understand gender norms as well as I could see my friends around me understood it. DG: There’s very little research in South Africa about same sex household, but international research shows that same sex households are just as suited to raising children as heterosexual ones. DG VO: Professor Carien Lubbe-De Beer, formerly of the University of Pretoria, is one of the few researchers compiling data on same sex parenting in South Africa. DG: Is there a stigma to being attached to a single sex family, for the children and for the parents? CL: I think as with any minority group, um, you’re different than the norm, you’re different than the mainstream, and people are, maybe due to not knowing, they are afraid of what’s this and then they go back to more fundamental core values DG: Perhaps the point is that the traditional definition of family is just… Traditional. It’s not new, and it’s not 2017. And that’s got to change. CL: And I think families are ever-changing. And we need to, we need to adapt to that. And we need to embrace the creativity of the different ways in which we can raise children. 40%, um, live with just their mothers, and 23%, um, only live with people that’s not even biologically related to them. DG VO: Even with a volunteer surrogate, Christo and Theo still had to approach the court to make an application for surrogacy. DG VO: Adele Van Der Walt is a practicing attorney specializing in medical law and one of the few experts on surrogacy law. DG: Are you seeing more and more same sex couples for surrogacy? AW: Definitely. Definitely. Since we’ve got the act, there’s legal clarity, certainty, for all parties. You approach court before the in vitro fertilization takes place, or the embryo transfer. They get a court order, and that court order confirms any baby or babies born from that relationship and contract is the lawful child of the intended parents, being the gay couple. DG: After 3 in vitro procedures and no viable pregnancy, the Menelaous went back to court. DG VO: On their fifth attempt, their surrogate fell pregnant… three times over. DG: What was that moment like when you found out you were going to have triplets? DM: [Laughing] I just laughed. I haven’t stopped giggling. And my husband said a few very long swear words. TM: We went to the lady. She started scanning, and it was, this is number one, this is number two, and she was juggling around, and then it was number three. DG VO: The happy news was short lived, as they would find out a few weeks later during a routine test/ appointment. TM: On 10 weeks, the doctor said to us, ‘Listen guys, this is not a happy day for me, but you guys need to abort.’ CM: Multiple pregnancies, especially triplets, is very high risk. They thought the one baby was piggybacking on the other baby, and one will be late in the pregnancy, let’s say 28, 25 weeks cause a total miscarriage. TM: He said, ‘You know the safest is to let go of the twins and to keep on with, with the single pregnancy.’ TM: And, um, he actually booked a termination date for us, for the twins, which was a week later. TM: And when we walked out of there, we were shattered. And we said, you know, but we just can’t do this. DG VO: The couple sought other opinions. A subsequent scan showed that the risk of miscarriage was minimal. Their surrogate would help them make the final decision. CM: We as parents, as the, the parents only from when the babies is born. The surrogate has got all rights which they still in the stomach. So if she decided on 12 weeks to terminate, she was legally allowed. Um, it’s not our, it’s not our choice. She always stood back and said, ‘I’m just the oven. It’s your decision.’ So, we’re blessed with our surrogate. DG VO: In July 2016, Christo and Theo’s surrogate gave birth to a boy -- Joshua -- and twin girls -- Zoe and Kate. DG VO: What makes their situation unique is that both fathers are genetically related to one or two of the children -- Christo to Joshua, and Theo to Zoe and Kate. DG VO: However, Zoe, one of the twin girls, was born with a heart condition that would prove more urgent than either of the fathers realized. TM: It was end of August, um, she crashed. At home. The one morning. And I rushed off to hospital close by. I didn’t even put her in the car seat. Um, I held her against my chest just to make sure she breathes. And she’s there, that I could actually feel her. And, um, yeah after working on her for 3 hours, they airlifted her to the hospital in Johannesburg. DG VO: After this initial scare, Zoe would undergo open heart surgery to begin repairing the defects in her heart. CM: The surgery was a 2 hour surgery, which ended up and 8 and a half hour surgery. And they couldn’t even close her chest open, they left the chest open and just closed it with plaster. They told us we have to prepare ourselves for the worst. DG VO: Zoe would pull through, but she would require future surgeries to fully address her medical issues. TM: But I think when you’re there, it’s like the world is ending and you just don’t know where to go. Um, because you’re helpless. I mean, there’s nothing you can do to make this better. CM: She’s gonna have another follow up surgery. We not prepared, but we know about it. In 2 weeks time. DG VO: While society seems to be adapting well to the Menelaous and the Shapiros, others in South Africa still face obstacles. CL: It has been quite tricky to make inroads into the lower socioeconomic strata, and, um, especially the, in terms of race. But just people also fearing for their lives. It’s really difficult in some areas of South Africa that people are afraid to be who they are, um, with the violence and the possibility of losing your life. DG VO: Back at the Menelaou home, Christo and Theo’s family is like any other. CM: Our surrogate is still, there’s an open door for her. She stays very nearby. DG VO: But their surrogate has her own family and children, and though she gave birth to them, she isn’t the triplets’ mother. DG: What advice do you have for other same sex couples that want to start a family? CM: My advice would be go for it. There’s nothing different. Um, we’ve got the same rights, we’ve got the same heart. The other day, me and Theo said, we said like, we’re gonna become like grandparents one day. We didn’t thought about that. Like a few weeks ago, like oh no, they gonna be opa and oma. [Laughing] TM: I will tell them to never look back. Because that will be the best decision they will ever make. There is nothing better that can happen to your life than being blessed with a child.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Families come in all shapes and sizes, but what happens when the traditional notion of a nuclear family begins to shift as same sex parenting and surrogacy becomes more prevalent?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Christo and Theo Menelaou made international news when their surrogate delivered triplets in July 2016. Now Carte Blanche brings an exclusive update on the triplet’s progress, their first birthday, and delves into issues surrounding surrogacy and same sex parenting.
metadata.Summary: In “2 Dads, 3 Babies,” we’ll spend a day in the life of Christo Menelaou, who owns a construction business in Pretoria. A wedding ring on his finger indicates he’s happily married, and as we arrive home with him, we meet his partner -- Theo. No ordinary same sex couple, last year Christo and Theo fulfilled their quest to become parents with the help of surrogate. She just happened to deliver triplets: Joshua, and twins Zoe and Kate. As we spend a day with Menelaou family, we’ll see the human stories behind same sex parenting and surrogacy. Though same sex parents still face stigma in society, the tide is beginning to change. We’ll take a step back and explain the legal process that South Africa has in place for surrogacy and then speak with a researcher who's done extensive work looking at the changing notion of ‘family’ in South Africa and what that means to society. Recent studies have shown no significant difference between children raised in same sex homes and those raised in heterosexual ones. The findings are that as long as the core relationship between the parents is strong and healthy, children will thrive. The notion of family as a man, woman, and children is currently in a state of upheaval. And with that, we’ll meet two adults who are the product of same sex homes: brothers with 2 lesbian mothers who were born via invitro fertilization in the 80s -- Samuel, who is straight and now married to a woman, and his brother Ben, who is gay. Samuel now works for a gay rights advocacy group, doing work that he says comes naturally to him since he spent his formative years educating others and helping them shed their homophobia. Finally, we’ll return to the Menelaou family. Christo, Theo, Joshua, Kate, and Zoe are just starting out in this world. With research and case studies on their side for a bright future, will the rest of South Africa be there as well?
metadata.Further information: We open on the Menelaou family -- Christo, Theo, and their triplets: Joshua, and twins Kate and Zoe. As we hear from the couple about the journey to becoming fathers, we’ll also get to experience a day in the life with the family. The truly unique way they all came together -- through the generosity of a woman, who would become their surrogate, that they met at the trial for their former neighbor and friend Oscar Pistorius -- may be starkly different from the “traditional family” model, but theirs is just the same. Infants fuss and make a mess, and stressed out parents figure it out on the fly. We’ll watch them prepare for a big day: the triplets first birthday, what they’ve decided will be a lowkey affair with just photos and cake. We’ll then hear from Adele Van Der Walt, a lawyer specializing in medical law and surrogacy. She’ll walk us through the legal aspects of the arrangement, especially as they pertain to same sex couples: everything from how a surrogate is connected to a couple to ethics issues that may arise, and even emotional issues. Though the legal process for surrogacy in South Africa is quite regimented, the psychological and emotional side of it is anything but. Back with the Menelaou family, Christo and Theo talk about daughter Kate, who was born with a heart condition that required open heart surgery in November 2016 (when she was only a few months old; they had to wait until she was 4kg to proceed with the surgery) and will require a follow up procedure next month. Though the joy of becoming fathers has provided for an intensely emotional year, Kate’s health has also been a major concern, demonstrating that a parent’s concern for their child’s health is universal, no matter what your sexual orientation. Carien Lubbe-De Beer, a professor of psychology at the University of Pretoria -- now based in New Zealand with her family -- has been researching the changing notion of ‘family’ in South Africa for many years, especially as it relates to same sex couples and their children. She’s published numerous papers detailing her work, including how “gay people are increasingly opting for motherhood and fatherhood by creating families of their own or by continuing to live with their children from former heterosexual relationships.” In the case studies that follow, we’ll meet now-grown children of both types of same sex families and hear their experiences growing up. Case studies will demonstrate that there’s no one single type of this new family. Samuel Shapiro was born to lesbian mothers through in vitro fertilization. Now, at the age of 29 and married to a woman, he’s dedicated his career to being an activist to advance equality and freedom in southern Africa with a particular emphasis on sexual orientation and gender identity. Not only will he speak of his personal experiences growing up in a same sex household, he’ll be a key voice in explaining how we can all do our part to help shed the stigma that is still too-often attached to families with same sex parents. We’ll also speak to his older brother Ben, who is gay, and what it was like growing up in a household with two moms and no significant male figures in his life. How did his upbringing shape who he’s become today? With the Meneloaus one final time, we see Christo and Theo working together to take care of the triplets. We’ll hear about their hopes and dreams for the children, tempered yet with some nerves about Kate’s upcoming surgery. Theirs may look different and may have come into being in a different way, but their family is just like any other. [Possibly end with Samuel Shapiro: “Gay parents are starting to be accepted… Not only can the world be different, but it’s happening. Change is inevitable.”]
